title: Upasiva's question (Sn 5)
hook: read it: what can I rely on to cross?
tomorrow: in the middle of a flood, is there anywhere to stand?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dhotaka's question: I can't free you, the Buddha said; know the teaching and cross yourself. So if you have to cross alone, what do you hold onto?

A first swim lesson. The kid clutches the edge of the pool, then the teacher's arm, then a foam board, anything solid. The next student on the way to the far shore, Upasiva, asks for exactly that. Alone, he says, with nothing to lean on, I can't cross this great flood. Give me a support, something to rely on. And the Buddha's answer is the odd detail. The support he offers is nothingness. Why would anyone hand a drowning man nothing?
screen: `CLUTCHING THE EDGE OF THE POOL.` → `GIVE ME A SUPPORT.` → `HE OFFERS NOTHINGNESS.`

segments.voice: In Upasiva's question the Buddha says: mindful, looking to nothingness, relying on the thought there is nothing, cross the flood. Let go of sense pleasures, give up doubting talk, and watch craving end, night and day. Here's the solve. Upasiva asked for a support, and the word, arammana, also means an object the mind rests on, the way a meditator rests on the breath. So the Buddha gives him one: a place for the mind to rest that isn't another thing to clutch. Every other support, a person, a plan, a possession, can be grabbed, and whatever you grab is one more thing to drag across. Nothingness can't be grabbed. Leaning on it, you let go. The swimmer's last lesson is the same: you float when you stop clutching. Then Upasiva pushes. What happens to the one who gets there? The answer is a picture worth keeping: like a flame blown out by the wind, it goes to rest and can't be counted; so the sage, freed from name and body, goes to rest and can't be counted. And when Upasiva asks whether that means he doesn't exist, the Buddha says there's no measure for such a one; every way of speaking about him has fallen away. So what I rely on, in this poem, is not a thing at all. It's the letting go.
screen: `MINDFUL, LOOKING TO NOTHINGNESS.` · `A REST THAT CAN'T BE CLUTCHED.` · `LIKE A FLAME BLOWN OUT.` · `NO MEASURE FOR SUCH A ONE.` · then, large: `WHAT I RELY ON.`

segments.voice: Let the chair or the floor hold you completely, as if you'd just stopped carrying yourself. Notice where it takes your weight: the back, the seat, the feet. Then, for the rest of the sit, let even the noticing go, and rest on nothing in particular, only the breath coming and going on its own.
Upasiva's question: alone and unable to cross, a student asks for a support. The Buddha points him to nothingness, a rest that can't be clutched, and to the flame that goes out.
A line to lean on: what I rely on is less, not more. Day sixteen seventy-five, afloat.

screen: `DAY 1675 COUNTS.` → `THE WAY TO THE FAR SHORE · 4 OF 8.` → `TOMORROW: IS THERE ANYWHERE TO STAND?`

howItsDone: In Theravada meditation, the base of nothingness is a deep, formless absorption; Upasiva's question is also read for its image of the freed sage as a flame gone out, beyond reckoning.

notes: Upasiva's question paraphrased (Sn 5.7 in the common numbering). Confirm: 'alone, without support, I can't cross the great flood; tell me a support (arammana)'; the answer: contemplating nothingness (akincanna), mindful, relying on 'there is nothing', cross the flood; abandon sense pleasures, refrain from doubts/talk, watch the ending of craving night and day; the flame simile (as a flame thrown by the force of wind goes to rest and can't be reckoned, so the sage released from name-and-body); and 'there is no measure of one who has gone to rest; all paths of speech are removed'.
Puzzle shape: the odd detail is that the 'support' offered is nothingness; the solve plays on arammana as both support and meditation object. Confirm that reading is fair.
The swimmer's floating image is the script's own, not the text's.
